doc.title: Ann Rabson interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, September 21, 2007

title: Why she records: In a Family Way and legacy
summary: She records so people remember her, made the family album for posterity, and began recording because earlier pianists left little behind.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: Is it worth it? Let’s see how to I ask this? If you’re thinking of doing another recording, you’re going to put out another CD, what is the main reason for doing it nowadays?

Well it depends on the CD. I am thinking about putting out another CD. And the reason is that I would like people to remember that I’m here. You know I’d like to be on the radio, I’d like to be available or have something out there so that I can be nominated for an award, I’d like people to hear me and think, “Oh yeah, let’s hire her.” You know. That’s part of the reason for this new CD. Part of it is because I have a lot of originals that I’ve never really been happy with the way that they were done and I want to do them again. Or I’ve got some new ones that I want to do. So this one’s going to be all originals. But the album before this one has an even more interesting background. It’s called “In a Family Way,” it’s all my family. And at holidays, you know Thanksgiving, we get together and when other families start bickering, we all pick up instruments and start playing. And I just — it’s so joyful, that experience, and so musical and so varied, that I just really wanted that saved for posterity.

The first recording that I did solo, which was really late in my career, for a long time I didn’t believe in recording because I mean I had opportunities but I just felt like Mary Martin felt about videotaping, that it’s going to take away from live performance. And you know what? I was right. I mean look at, people are staying home and — anyway. But that first recording I did, I did because I was cussing a lot of musicians. Well Jimmy Yancy and Big Maceo and all these wonderful musicians who had not recorded very much in their lifetimes and didn’t leave a legacy for me. And I was angry. And I thought wait a minute, maybe people are going to feel that way about me someday. You know Pinetop Smith is the real one was just four cuts or something. Louise Johnson, same
thing, four cuts. But anyway so that was the reason I first started recording was I thought maybe somebody might want to hear.
